routes.description: Establish that consciousness, intentionality, agency, and personal identity cannot be exhausted by physical descriptions, then identify a single nonphysical subject capable of persisting independently of its present body and entering later embodiment.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the mental features and identity conditions require a nonphysical bearer, bodily dependence is compatible with that bearer's continued existence, and a coherent mechanism or argument supports survival beyond bodily death.

motionBridge.description: Show that a conscious person includes one nonphysical subject whose identity can continue after the present organism dies.

centralBridges.description: Establish that phenomenal character or intrinsic intentionality is not captured by an exclusively physical inventory.
Connect irreducible mental properties to a single subject that bears and unifies the person's mental states.
Supply identity conditions under which that subject can remain the same person across bodily discontinuity or renewed embodiment.
Explain why dependence of embodied capacities on the brain does not entail destruction of the subject when the brain ceases functioning.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use reason-responsive agency or freedom to reinforce the distinction between mentality and bottom-up physical causation.
Provide cosmological or probabilistic support for recurrence or another opportunity for postmortem embodiment.

routes.description: Account for consciousness, intentionality, agency, and personal unity as properties or activities of natural organisms at appropriate explanatory scales, while challenging any inference from mental distinctiveness to a separable enduring substance.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalistic organism-level explanations accommodate the cited mental phenomena, brain dependence undermines an independently functioning bearer, and the proposed identity or cosmological grounds for postmortem survival are not required.

motionBridge.description: Show that the conscious person is a natural organism and that no independently surviving nonphysical subject is needed.

centralBridges.description: Explain mental properties at the organismic scale without reducing them to microphysical vocabulary or adding another substance.
Give physicalist-compatible accounts of phenomenal knowledge, intentional attitudes, and unified consciousness.
Use the systematic dependence of mental capacities on brain states and integrity to oppose separable personal existence.
Challenge the identity conditions and cosmological premises offered to support recurrence or postmortem persistence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Preserve deliberation and reason-responsive action through compatibilist or higher-scale causal explanation.
Relate the onset and loss of conscious capacities to the presence of suitable neural organization.

sections.title: Phenomenal consciousness and physical explanation
sections.rationale: The status of qualia and phenomenal knowledge determines whether first-person experience supplies evidence for facts or properties beyond a natural physical account.

sections.title: Intentionality, mental causation, and agency
sections.rationale: Competing accounts of aboutness, reason-responsive action, and higher-level causation test whether mental activity requires a nonphysical source or fits an organismic framework.

sections.title: From nonphysical properties to subjects and personal identity
sections.rationale: The motion concerns substances rather than merely unusual properties, making the inference to a unified subject and its criteria of persistence an indispensable burden.

sections.title: Cosmology, recurrence, and postmortem survival
sections.rationale: The temporal probability argument, recurrence mechanism, and rival cosmological models bear on whether personal existence can recur after bodily death.

sections.title: Brain dependence, embodiment, and disembodied capacity
sections.rationale: Evidence concerning brain impairment, suitable neural conditions, and the capacities of a disembodied subject bears directly on separability and survival.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Qualia resist physical reduction because their felt first-person character is itself the phenomenon requiring explanation, unlike the mental effects of externally reduced phenomena such as heat.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly addresses Huemer, and the uninterrupted answer presents his stated argument from qualia.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes the first-person character of qualia as an explanandum and contrasts it with ordinary external reductions; it has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly develops a central premise and an illuminating contrast, though it does not complete the anti-physicalist inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The qualia claim and heat comparison are recoverable and stable, with the limitation from explanatory resistance to metaphysical irreducibility left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The language presents physical explanation as difficult rather than claiming a demonstrated impossibility, fitting the introspective support supplied.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The contrast coherently isolates felt character as the outstanding explanandum, but the bridge from explanatory difficulty to irreducibility remains bounded and implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: First-person accessibility and the heat analogy provide relevant support, though no systematic comparison with reductive or representational accounts is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central mental-nonphysicality bridge, while stopping short of establishing a substance or survivor.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily states its own explanandum and does not substantially characterize a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt stresses first-person acquaintance, inability to know what an unfamiliar experience is like, and difficulty stating qualia in physical terms.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Mary's acquisition of experiential knowledge is compatible with identity theory because fully knowing certain physical brain states may require occupying those states.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator turns directly to Oppy, whose extended answer identifies his identity theory and applies it to the Mary case.

components.text: Whether first-person experiential access is incompatible with physical identity.

response.rationale: The reply directly offers a physicalist-compatible explanation of privileged experiential knowledge: complete knowledge of a brain state may require occupying that very state.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the first-person-access premise and supplies a clear identity-theoretic compatibility account.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between identifying a state physically and fully knowing it through occupation is clear, stable, and explicitly conditional.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reply advances compatibility rather than claiming conclusive proof of identity theory, matching the conceptual warrant provided.

charity.alternative: Experiential knowledge reveals a nonphysical qualitative fact absent from complete physical knowledge.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply must explain novelty without merely redescribing Mary's epistemic gain.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from state identity to occupation-dependent full knowledge is consistent and directly explains why prior descriptive knowledge may be incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The account is supported by a specific Mary-case application, but the crucial claim that some physical states require occupation is asserted rather than independently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central phenomenal-functional bridge by giving a physicalist-compatible account of experiential knowledge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It fairly preserves the novelty of experience while locating that novelty in state acquaintance, though it does not fully address a determinate new-fact formulation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Oppy identifies perceptual states largely with brain states and asks whether their experiential dimension can be fully known only while one occupies them.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Reality contains scale-specific properties that cannot be defined from lower-scale properties, without making the lower scale metaphysically privileged or abandoning naturalism.
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy announces that he will explain his own view and delivers a sustained first-person account of properties across physical scales.

components.text: Whether failure of lower-scale definition requires a nonphysical ontology.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the reduction demand by denying that naturalism privileges the lowest scale and by allowing autonomous properties at chemical and other scales.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly answers the inference from nonreducibility to nonphysicality, although it does not provide a detailed phenomenal account.

precisionFindings.rationale: The multiscale thesis is recoverable and its key terms remain stable, but the range and individuation of relevant scales are only partly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents a general naturalistic framework with acknowledged uncertainty over examples and scale terminology, fitting its illustrative support.

charity.alternative: Qualia are distinctive because their first-person character is not merely another autonomous higher-scale property.
charity.decisiveQualification: A multiscale framework must still explain why phenomenal character belongs within the natural hierarchy.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The denial of microphysical privilege coherently permits irreducible higher-scale natural properties without adding substances, with one implicit emergence bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Chemical and other scale examples illustrate the framework, but representative evidence and a defended application to consciousness remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move strongly advances multiscale naturalism, a central bridge, while only indirectly explaining phenomenal character itself.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly blocks a generic inference from autonomy to dualism, but gives only a compressed application to the special phenomenal case.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes autonomy at the chemical scale and generalizes it to other scales while denying that lower-scale definability fixes naturalistic status.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Mary gains propositional knowledge of a determinate qualitative property, not merely an ability, because seeing red rules out alternative ways that the experience could have felt.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly solicits Huemer's response, and Huemer directly contrasts his fact-based interpretation with Oppy's skills account.

components.text: Whether Mary's epistemic gain is merely occupation-dependent acquaintance or ability.

response.rationale: The reply directly argues that Mary's experience rules out alternative qualitative possibilities and therefore supplies propositional knowledge that seeing red is like this.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the opponent's epistemic interpretation and supplies a determinate-worlds test for treating the gain as factual.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claimed new fact, its determinate qualitative content, and the contrast with abilities or acquaintance are clearly recoverable and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Ruling out qualitative alternatives supports propositional novelty, but the further conclusion that the fact is nonphysical is not established in this span.

charity.alternative: Mary gains a new mode of acquaintance with an old physical fact rather than a new fact.
charity.decisiveQualification: Ruling out possibilities must distinguish new propositional content from a new presentation of existing content.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move coherently infers propositional knowledge from evidence that excludes qualitative alternatives, leaving one bounded bridge concerning modes of presentation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The alternative-possibilities test is specific and relevant, but it does not independently show that the acquired fact lies outside the physical inventory.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central physicalist account of phenomenal knowledge and reinforces the nonphysicality route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately engages the acquaintance alternative and offers a modal answer, though it does not fully resolve the old-fact/new-mode distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer says Mary learns that seeing red is like this and that her new evidence excludes ways the qualitative character could instead have been.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Qualia and intentionality support property dualism, while the problem of personal identity provides the further route from nonphysical properties to substance dualism.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly directs the intentionality question to Huemer, and the uninterrupted answer develops his stated dualist argument.

response.rationale: This constructive move expressly separates support for nonphysical properties from the further personal-identity route needed to establish a substance that bears them.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it accurately identifies an indispensable bridge but only announces, rather than executes, the property-to-substance inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: Property dualism, substance dualism, and the proposed role of personal identity are distinguished clearly, with the incompleteness of the route acknowledged.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The route is presented cautiously, but saying substance dualism is not much further understates the major bearer and identity conditions still required.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between property and substance dualism is coherent, but personal identity is named rather than supplied as the material inferential bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Qualia and intentionality are cited as support for properties, while the decisive transition to a substance receives little argument or evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It expressly reaches the indispensable central subject-from-properties bridge, despite leaving that bridge substantially incomplete.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move mainly maps its own argumentative route and does not materially characterize a developed opposing position.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer says qualia and intentionality indicate nonphysical properties and that personal identity is needed to proceed from dualism generally to substance dualism.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Tree rings have no intrinsic aboutness; they function as evidence only because observers interpret them through mental states that represent the tree's age.
moves.attributionBasis: The exchange directly follows a challenge posed to Huemer, and his answer distinguishes intrinsic from derivative intentionality.

components.text: Whether autonomous natural properties can accommodate mentality without another substance.

response.rationale: The tree-ring example bears on naturalistic intentionality but does not address the decisive multiscale claim; it instead distinguishes interpreted evidence from intrinsic mental aboutness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it offers substantive contrary material about derivative representation but leaves the target's scale-specific naturalism untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The tree-ring example and distinction between derivative and intrinsic intentionality are clearly stated with stable scope and terminology.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker cautiously offers interpretation by observers as the best account of tree-ring aboutness, matching the example's limited warrant.

charity.alternative: Tree rings possess natural informational aboutness independently of a particular observer's occurrent interpretation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Informational covariance may be genuine while still differing from intrinsic semantic content.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The observer-interpretation explanation consistently distinguishes evidential use from intrinsic aboutness, with one implicit premise about what genuine representation requires.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The concrete tree-ring case supports the distinction, but broader exclusion of naturalized intrinsic intentionality is not defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the central mental-nonphysicality issue through intentionality, but less directly than the phenomenal arguments.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response recognizes derivative intentionality and targets the semantic distinction, though it compresses stronger teleosemantic or informational alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer says rings are not literally about anything and become evidence of age because an observer has a mental state representing the tree as old.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Functionalist accounts can explain intentional attitudes within identity theory, making intentionality less troublesome for physicalism than consciousness or qualia.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly hands the discussion to Oppy, whose answer contrasts physicalist treatments of intentionality with the harder qualia problem.

components.text: Whether intentional attitudes require irreducible intrinsic mental aboutness.

response.rationale: The reply directly offers identity-theoretic functionalism as a physicalist-compatible account of beliefs, desires, and their aboutness, while distinguishing the harder qualia issue.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly contacts the intentionality challenge and names an alternative explanatory framework, though the framework's mechanism is only summarized.

precisionFindings.rationale: The limited claim that intentionality is less problematic than qualia and can receive a functionalist account is clear and appropriately scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reply claims a reasonable account rather than a decisive reduction, appropriately matching its compressed appeal to functionalism.

charity.alternative: Functional roles capture causal use but not the intrinsic content by which a thought is about its object.
charity.decisiveQualification: Naming functionalism must address the intrinsic-versus-derivative distinction rather than merely causal organization.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Identity theory and functional role can coherently coexist at different explanatory levels, but the bridge from function to semantic content remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move cites an established style of account and representative attitudes, yet supplies little internal defense of how function constitutes aboutness.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports a physicalist-compatible account of intentional attitudes, though phenomenal consciousness remains expressly unresolved.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply does not caricature the dualist concern, but it leaves the decisive intrinsic-content qualification largely unaddressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: Oppy says identity theorists may also be functionalists and that functionalism gives a reasonable account of intentional attitudes such as belief and desire.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Macroscopic indeterminacy does not yield libertarian freedom, while action from normally acquired beliefs and desires without defeating interference supplies sufficient compatibilist freedom.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly asks Oppy for his response, and the sustained answer states both his indeterminist cosmology and compatibilist account of agency.

components.text: Whether physical causes can possess the reason-responsive content required for agency.

response.rationale: The reply gives a substantive naturalistic account of freedom but does not directly answer intrinsic intentionality; it shifts to acting on normally acquired beliefs and desires without interference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it advances issue-bearing agency material but leaves the selected target's intrinsic-aboutness demand uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: Libertarian and compatibilist freedom are clearly distinguished, and the proposed no-interference condition is stated with stable scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents an inclined compatibilist view rather than certainty, fitting the conceptual account and acknowledged cosmological uncertainty.

charity.alternative: Freedom requires an agent able to do otherwise in a stronger libertarian sense.
charity.decisiveQualification: A compatibilist replacement must preserve deliberative control rather than merely describe caused behavior.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move coherently denies that indeterminacy supplies control and offers a reason-guided compatibilist condition, with one bounded account-of-normal-acquisition gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual contrast is relevant and specific, but no substantial evidence is offered for the sufficiency of the proposed freedom condition.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary natural-agency bridge, at the upper end of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly distinguishes the stronger alternative and identifies beliefs, desires, and absence of defeating interference as its control-preserving substitute.

moves.evidenceBasis: Oppy rejects strong libertarian freedom and defines free action through normally acquired beliefs and desires operating without relevant interference or compulsion.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Emergent or downward-causal organization does not establish substance dualism because higher-scale events remain events occurring in the brain, without an additional mental substance.
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy answers the suggestion that dualists would claim victory and explicitly distinguishes the emergent story from the existence of mental substances.

components.text: Whether higher-level mental properties entail an additional mental substance.

response.rationale: The reply directly rejects the property-to-substance inference: higher-scale or downward-causal events remain brain events and introduce no additional bearer into the account.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive inference from mental-level organization to a distinct substance, though its positive ontology remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The denial of an extra substance and identification of higher-scale events as brain events are concise, recoverable, and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical denial follows within Oppy's stipulated multiscale story, but does not independently exclude every substance-dualist interpretation.

charity.alternative: Downward causation may require a mental substance that acts upon brain processes.
charity.decisiveQualification: Distinct causal organization does not by itself establish a numerically distinct bearer.

logicalCoherence.rationale: It validly blocks an inference from higher-scale causation to an extra substance by locating the relevant events in the brain, with one ownership premise implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The ontology is plainly stated but supported largely by assertion in this short span rather than detailed evidence or rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the indispensable central bridge from nonphysical or emergent properties to a separate subject.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply isolates the decisive property-versus-substance distinction accurately, although it offers only a brief positive account of event ownership.

moves.evidenceBasis: Oppy states that no mental substance appears in the emergent story because what occurs at the human scale is still happening in the brain.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: If time is infinite in both directions and each person lives only once, the probability of being alive now is zero; therefore reincarnation occurs or the infinite-past assumption is false.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly invites Huemer to present his argument, and the ensuing uninterrupted answer uses his stated assumptions and conclusion.

response.rationale: This constructive move offers cosmological support through a dilemma: given a two-way infinite timeline, a unique finite life would allegedly make present existence probability zero.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it supplies an explicit conditional structure but leaves the probability measure and connection to personal recurrence underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The dilemma and assumptions are explicit, but the reference class for probability over temporal locations is not stably specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Although framed conditionally, the zero-probability claim lacks a defended measure over infinite time and overstates what the assumptions alone establish.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The stated dilemma is intelligible, but it relies on an unsupported uniform probability over infinite temporal positions and risks a false dichotomy.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The fact-dependent and measure-dependent probability conclusion is asserted without a defined sampling process, base rate, or defended cosmological premise.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary cosmological bridge and is highly consequential within that tier, but does not itself establish identity-preserving survival.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move constructs its own probabilistic dilemma without substantially presenting or evaluating a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer explicitly assumes one life and time infinite in both directions, then says the probability of being alive specifically now appears to be zero.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Contemporary cosmology makes a finite past and infinite future more plausible than an infinite past, while expansion and entropy considerations also undermine cosmic recurrence.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly contrasts Huemer's temporal view with the view favored by physics and supplies cosmological and entropy-based considerations.

components.text: Whether the two-way infinite-time premise required by the probability dilemma is credible.
Whether physical cosmology supplies recurrent conditions for later embodiment.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the premise failure and its consequence: a finite past removes the two-way-infinite setup, while entropy and expansion undercut the recurrence mechanism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly attacks both the temporal premise and the separate recurrence component, stating why the original dilemma loses its physical basis.

precisionFindings.rationale: Finite-past plausibility and anti-recurrence considerations are clearly separated and presented as comparative cosmological judgments.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move says current physics favors rather than proves the finite-past model and treats recurrence as a distinct question.

charity.alternative: Time may be infinite in both directions even if standard cosmological models favor a finite past.
charity.decisiveQualification: Comparative physical plausibility defeats reliance on the premise without demonstrating metaphysical impossibility.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The finite-past objection directly removes a required premise, and the separate entropy objection coherently challenges recurrence without conflating the two points.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The appeal to contemporary cosmology, expansion, and entropy is specific and representative, though detailed model documentation is absent from the span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the subsidiary cosmological-support bridge at the top of that tier and substantially weakens the recurrence argument.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply maintains the distinction between implausibility and impossibility and separately addresses recurrence, with only limited model detail.

moves.evidenceBasis: Oppy contrasts the infinite-past view with the finite-past, infinite-future model favored by physics and separately raises entropy and recurrence concerns.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Standard projections of an eternally expanding universe imply eventual proton and black-hole decay followed only by sparse radiation, so stars, people, and recurrent conditions never return.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker answers Huemer's finite-cycling premise and describes the long-term cosmological future presented as the serious physical projection.

components.text: Whether an infinite future generates recurrent physical conditions for persons.

response.rationale: The reply directly denies recurrence by describing continued expansion, proton and black-hole decay, and a radiation-only future in which stars and people do not return.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the recurrence mechanism with a concrete rival projection and a clear defeating consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The long-run cosmological sequence and its consequence for recurrence are specific, stable, and scoped to standard projections.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The projection is presented as the serious standard future rather than an absolute metaphysical certainty, matching the scientific warrant invoked.

charity.alternative: An infinite future may eventually reproduce any finite physical configuration.
charity.decisiveQualification: Infinite duration does not ensure recurrence when expansion and irreversible decay continually alter accessible conditions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The physical sequence from expansion and decay to increasingly sparse radiation directly supports the stated absence of recurrent stars and persons.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It provides concrete standard-cosmology milestones and mechanisms, with only a bounded lack of documentation and model-alternative comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It very strongly attacks the subsidiary cosmological bridge, while not addressing noncosmological survival mechanisms.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately confronts the infinity-to-recurrence inference and supplies the decisive physical qualification rather than dismissing infinity alone.

moves.evidenceBasis: Oppy describes proton decay, final black-hole evaporation, continuing expansion, and sparse radiation, expressly concluding that protons, stars, and people do not return.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Blind bottom-up physical causes cannot ground free will because they do not respond to reasons, whereas causation by a higher-level mental subject can make conduct reason-responsive.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly directs the question to Huemer, and the ensuing first-person answer restates and develops Huemer's earlier free-will argument.

components.text: Whether acting from beliefs and desires supplies genuine reason-responsive freedom.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges the compatibilist account by arguing that bottom-up physical causes themselves lack reasons and therefore cannot make behavior genuinely reason-responsive.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the proposed compatibilist mechanism and supplies a higher-level mental-cause alternative, though it does not fully analyze realization relations.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast between blind physical causes and a reason-responsive mental subject is clear, but 'higher level' shifts between causal scale and ontological subject.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling a separate higher-level mental cause the only route to freedom exceeds the supplied argument and omits physical realization alternatives.

charity.alternative: Physical systems can respond to reasons when organism-level representational states realize deliberation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Microphysical constituents need not individually possess reasons for the organized person to be reason-responsive.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move identifies a genuine explanatory demand but commits a substantial composition-style leap from reasonless microcauses to nonresponsive higher-level behavior.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conclusion relies mainly on assertion about bottom-up causes and does not compare physicalist accounts of representation, realization, or reasons as causes.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary agency bridge and sits at the top of that relevance tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply materially weakens the compatibilist alternative by attributing the blindness of microcauses directly to the organized person's causal capacities.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer says physical causes are blind and do not respond to reasons, then claims freedom requires causation by the higher-level mental thing.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: A resemblance-based account of personal identity does not readily support reincarnation as an animal because an animal would not be a qualitative duplicate of the person.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly challenges Huemer's reincarnation proposal by invoking the resemblance and duplication conditions from Huemer's own personal-identity argument.

components.text: Whether infinite time and present existence support recurrence of the same person.

response.rationale: The reply raises a material identity objection concerning animal embodiment, but it does not address the dilemma's probability premise or establish why temporal recurrence fails generally.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it supplies a significant identity-condition objection while leaving the selected cosmological inference itself uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The resemblance criterion, qualitative-duplicate condition, and cross-species counterexample are clearly recoverable and appropriately limited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker says the animal case is unclear rather than impossible, appropriately matching the resemblance-based objection.

charity.alternative: A persisting soul, rather than qualitative resemblance, could preserve identity across species.
charity.decisiveQualification: The objection applies to the resemblance-based route and does not by itself defeat a soul-based identity criterion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If qualitative duplication plays the proposed identity role, a markedly dissimilar animal embodiment presents a coherent and material counterexample.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The dog comparison concretely tests the stated resemblance condition, though the underlying identity theory is only briefly reconstructed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central personal-persistence bridge by exposing a cross-species gap in the proposed identity condition.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately confines itself to the resemblance story, although the later soul alternative is not yet supplied in the targeted material.

moves.evidenceBasis: Oppy recalls the role of qualitative duplication in Huemer's identity account and observes that a dog is not sufficiently similar to the person.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Reincarnation need not depend on eternal recurrence or qualitative duplication, because unknown conditions might instead cause an enduring soul to enter another living organism.
moves.attributionBasis: Huemer recounts in the first person how multiverse duplication inspired his argument and then distinguishes that route from an alternative involving a persisting soul.

components.text: Whether cross-species reincarnation must satisfy a qualitative-duplication condition.
Whether cosmological recurrence is necessary for later embodiment.

response.rationale: The reply justifies replacing duplication and cosmic recurrence with persistence of a soul as the identity bearer, preserving the issue of same-person reembodiment while changing its mechanism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly explains why the resemblance and recurrence objections need not govern the soul-based route, but supplies no positive conditions for attachment.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between eternal recurrence and an alternative persisting-soul mechanism is explicit, stable, and carefully presented as possibility.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Unknown conditions are offered only as a possible alternative mechanism, which matches the deliberately limited support.

charity.alternative: Without duplication or recurrent physical conditions, no identity-preserving mechanism for reincarnation has been supplied.
charity.decisiveQualification: A persisting soul could provide identity, but its embodiment conditions still require an account.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A persisting bearer can coherently replace resemblance as the identity condition, but the attachment mechanism and bearer identity remain materially underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move establishes conceptual compatibility but relies expressly on unknown conditions and therefore supplies little evidential support for actual reembodiment.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central personal-persistence bridge, though it does not establish that reembodiment occurs.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly concedes that recurrence was one mechanism and identifies the exact remaining gap rather than treating bare possibility as explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer says eternal recurrence is not essential and proposes that an enduring soul might enter another living thing under presently unknown conditions.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: A soul is the single subject bearing all of a person's rational thoughts, sensations, and emotions, rather than an additional rational entity distinct from the ordinary subject of experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Huemer by name, and Huemer answers by explicitly defining what he means by a soul and applying that definition to rational thought, sensation, and emotion.

components.text: Whether the soul is an additional entity or the ordinary unified subject of experience.

response.rationale: The reply directly clarifies that the soul is not an extra rational agent beside the person but the one subject bearing rational, sensory, and emotional states.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the extra-substance objection by specifying the proposed bearer's unifying role, though it does not prove ontological separateness.

precisionFindings.rationale: The soul is consistently defined as the single subject of diverse mental states, with clear scope and no material terminological shift.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Unity of ordinary self-ascription supports one subject, but confident identification of that subject with a nonphysical soul exceeds the stated evidence.

charity.alternative: The organism or brain may be the single subject of all these mental states without a further soul.
charity.decisiveQualification: Mental unity identifies a bearer but does not by itself determine whether that bearer is physical.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The account consistently avoids duplication of subjects, but the inference from one experiential subject to a nonphysical substance leaves a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Unified ownership of thoughts, sensations, and emotions is relevant introspective support, but it underdetermines the bearer's physical status.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the indispensable central subject-from-properties bridge and specifies the proposed unifying bearer.

representationalCharity.rationale: The clarification avoids positing two experiencers, yet it does not adequately handle the strongest organismic interpretation of the same unity.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer rejects a separate rational soul and says the same me is the subject of rational thoughts, sensations, and emotions.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Souls have always existed rather than emerging through evolution, but a soul can inhabit an organism only when suitable physical conditions, such as a brain capable of supporting intelligence, arise.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly invites Huemer to clarify his answer, and Huemer states both the eternal existence of souls and the bodily conditions required for embodied life.

components.text: Whether identity across embodiment requires qualitative resemblance to the present person.

response.rationale: The move explains when a soul could inhabit an organism but does not answer the resemblance-based identity objection; neural suitability is issue-bearing embodiment material, not identity contact.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it materially addresses embodiment thresholds while leaving the selected personal-identity demand uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: Eternal souls and suitable bodily conditions are recoverable, but intelligence and brain support fluctuate as candidate thresholds without a settled criterion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker repeatedly acknowledges not knowing the precise conditions and offers neural intelligence only as a probable illustration.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Preexisting souls plus later suitable organisms form a consistent model, but no rule explains selection, attachment, or why intelligence is decisive.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The timing of intelligent brains is illustrative, while eternal existence and the soul-to-organism attachment condition remain unsupported speculation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It substantially supports the central survival-possibility bridge by separating existence from operative embodiment, despite an undeveloped mechanism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily clarifies its own speculative embodiment conditions and does not materially evaluate a developed contrary account.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer says souls always existed but could not inhabit objects or early organisms until brains capable of supporting intelligence arose, while admitting the conditions are unknown.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: A disembodied soul may survive bodily death while being unable to think or act, because brain damage impairs human capacities and death destroys the entire brain that supports them.
moves.attributionBasis: The follow-up question asks Huemer whether disembodied persons can think, and his answer appeals directly to the observed dependence of reasoning and other capacities on the brain.

components.text: Whether higher-scale brain events require a distinct nonphysical bearer.

response.rationale: The reply is relevant to separability but does not answer the ontology objection; it concedes total operational dependence while asserting that the inactive soul may persist.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it addresses survival under brain loss but leaves the earlier demand for evidence of a distinct bearer uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: Survival is clearly distinguished from the ability to think or act, and the claim is explicitly limited by 'as far as I know' language.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move cautiously claims only that survival without operation may occur and openly bases incapacity on brain dependence.

charity.alternative: If every observable mental capacity disappears with the brain, nothing personal remains to count as survival.
charity.decisiveQualification: Persistence without operation is conceptually possible but requires an independent identity criterion or evidence for the bearer.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between existence and operative capacity is coherent, but it does not establish that an inactive subject persists after all identifying functions cease.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Brain-damage evidence supports loss of capacities, not survival of the bearer; that decisive persistence claim remains largely unsupported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly reaches the central survival-possibility bridge by arguing that dependence of function does not entail destruction of the subject.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accepts the full force of operational dependence and distinguishes it from destruction, while leaving the persistence evidence unresolved.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer appeals to progressive impairment from brain damage and infers that total brain destruction ends all activity, while leaving the soul's existence possible.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Pervasive impairment from brain damage supports the conclusion that human capacities depend on the brain rather than an independently functioning soul.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly continues Oppy's brain-dependence response and contrasts people with the preceding Iron Man analogy.

components.text: Whether pervasive brain dependence is compatible with an independently functioning soul.
Whether suitable brains merely enable capacities of an otherwise independent soul.

response.rationale: The reply directly uses pervasive impairment evidence against the analogy of a complete person merely using a body, challenging both independent operation and mere-enablement accounts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive dependence evidence and its consequence, though it does not directly show that an inactive bearer cannot persist.

precisionFindings.rationale: The dependence thesis is clear, but the suggestion that everything people do can be impaired is broad and expressly acknowledged as an assumption.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Brain-damage correlations strongly support dependence of capacities, but extending them to every capacity and destruction of a bearer goes beyond the stated evidence.

charity.alternative: The brain may be an enabling interface whose damage blocks a soul's expression without damaging the soul itself.
charity.decisiveQualification: Functional dependence underdetermines whether the underlying bearer is destroyed or merely unable to operate.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Pervasive capacity impairment coherently counts against an independently functioning agent, while the inference from impaired manifestation to no bearer remains incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Brain-damage cases provide systematic relevant evidence, though the universal scope and metaphysical conclusion are not fully documented or defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central brain-dependence bridge and strongly challenges separable personal operation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly challenges the complete-agent analogy using human evidence, but does not resolve the interface interpretation's decisive qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Oppy contrasts a complete Iron Man outside the suit with human evidence that brain damage impairs what people can do, while acknowledging some uncertainty about universality.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Evidence linking relevant mental states to brain activity makes it reasonable to deny that a soul is attached to a fetus before the requisite neural activity develops.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the fetal-development question to Oppy, whose answer invokes empirical brain and mental-state correlations.

components.text: Whether soul attachment begins only when suitable neural organization exists.

response.rationale: The reply directly accepts a neural threshold structure but argues from brain-state correlations that no soul is attached before relevant fetal brain activity develops.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the proposed embodiment condition and supplies an empirical reason for locating attachment no earlier than relevant neural activity.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is clearly limited to the pre-threshold fetus, and uncertainty about the exact developmental point is expressly preserved.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Brain-mental correlations warrant confidence about absent mental capacities, but not confidence that no nonoperative soul is attached before neural activity.

charity.alternative: A soul may be attached before it can manifest mental states through an immature brain.
charity.decisiveQualification: Absence of neural correlates or manifested mentality does not by itself establish absence of a nonoperative bearer.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The neural-threshold inference is coherent for manifested mentality but substantially overreaches when used to deny attachment of a stipulated inactive soul.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Brain-mental correlations are relevant and substantial, yet they underdetermine the metaphysical presence of a bearer without current capacities.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary embodiment-threshold bridge and sits near the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply relies on manifestation evidence while omitting the opponent's explicit distinction between a soul's existence and its operative capacities.

moves.evidenceBasis: Oppy cites extensive links between brain activity and mental states, inferring no attached soul before relevant fetal neural activity while leaving the precise threshold open.
